Use the randomized county assignment `reminder_draw` as an instrument for turnout, estimating two-stage least squares with county and election-year fixed effects and respecting any strata in the annual random draws.  
The first stage relates turnout to reminder assignment, with the documented 2.4-percentage-point increase establishing relevance; the second stage relates incumbent-party vote share to instrumented turnout, reporting the reduced form, first-stage strength, and county-clustered uncertainty.  
Random assignment supports independence, while the nonpartisan content and absence of other program changes support exclusion; under exclusion, no spillovers, and monotonicity, the estimate captures the local turnout effect induced by reminders rather than the effect of every possible turnout intervention.  
Use `dem_prev` and pre-assignment `pop_density`, `pct_rural`, and `median_inc` only as optional precision controls, not as the source of identification.  
Reject `eday_rain` despite its negative first stage because the reported risk-aversion and incumbent-preference channel threatens exclusion by changing vote choice independently of turnout.  
The main threat to the reminder design is that reminders could themselves change incumbent preferences among otherwise-voters, or affect neighboring counties, so assess implementation records and spillovers without treating balance tests as proof of exclusion.

Estimate two-stage least squares with county and election-year fixed effects, first predicting turnout from assignment and then estimating incumbent-party vote share using instrumented turnout.
Report the assignment effect on vote share, the estimated first stage and its strength, and the IV effect in vote-share percentage points per turnout percentage point, with county-clustered inference respecting any additional features of the randomization.
Identification requires exclusion, no cross-county spillovers, and monotonicity; under heterogeneous effects, interpret the estimate as a local, instrument-specific effect of reminder-induced turnout rather than the effect of every possible turnout increase.
The main threat is that reminders change vote choice among people who would vote anyway, violating exclusion; election-day rainfall is another plausible instrument conditional on the fixed effects, but its nonrandom assignment makes it a less compelling primary design.

Use the 1992 village lottery as a randomized encouragement design, instrumenting log household income per adult equivalent with `transfer_draw × post_draw`, since assignment itself is absorbed by individual fixed effects.
Estimate two-stage least squares with individual and survey-round fixed effects, using reported illness episodes in the preceding four weeks as the outcome and aligning post-draw status with actual payment and interview dates.
The documented 0.12-log-point income increase establishes promising relevance, but report the estimated first stage, reduced-form health effect, and weak-instrument-robust confidence intervals, clustering inference at the village level.
The key exclusion restriction is that lottery assignment affects illness only through measured household income; the main threat is that recurring transfers change income security, expectations, or village-wide conditions beyond what contemporaneous household income captures, even though the fund changed no other program.
Check baseline balance and differential attrition, avoid controlling for post-transfer mediators, and interpret the estimate as the income effect induced by this transfer program rather than a universal income–health relationship.
Reject `season_rain` as an instrument because rainfall can directly affect malaria, waterborne disease, and other health risks despite individual and round fixed effects.

Report the first stage (the documented post-draw increase is 0.12 log points), the reduced-form effect on illness, and the IV estimate, with village-clustered inference and randomization-based inference respecting the 25-of-51 draw. Under exclusion, no cross-village spillovers, and monotonicity, interpret the estimate as a local income-response effect for households whose income rises because of assignment, not necessarily the population-average effect. The main threat is exclusion: although the fund changed nothing else, predictable transfers could affect health through security or behavior beyond measured contemporaneous income, so assess that possibility alongside differential attrition. Reject `season_rain` as an instrument because rainfall can affect illness directly through malaria, as the surveillance records document, and individual and round fixed effects do not remove that time-varying pathway.

Use the randomized public-works assignment, `works_draw`, as an instrument for rural income growth, rather than relying on selection-on-observables.
Estimate district- and year-fixed-effects 2SLS, instrumenting annual income growth with `works_draw` interacted with an indicator for years when the program operated after the 1985 draw; confirm implementation dates before defining that indicator.
The outcome is district-year riot counts, and the coefficient measures riots per one-percentage-point increase in program-induced income growth, with a local causal interpretation under exclusion, monotonicity, and no spillovers.
Report the first stage—the documented increase is 1.2 percentage points—the assignment effect on riots, district-clustered uncertainty, and randomization-based inference, using pre-draw outcomes to check balance and placebo effects.
Reject `monsoon_dev` because deficit monsoons increase riots even where irrigation insulates crop income, contradicting exclusion; the main remaining threat is that public works affect riots through employment, infrastructure, or neighboring districts rather than measured income growth alone, although the codebook explicitly rules out other program changes.
